title: Weight-loss drugs in sport: Ozempic, Mounjaro not on Wada banned list for athletes
description: Semaglutide, often marketed under the Ozempic and Wegovy banners, was first placed on Wada's monitoring list in 2024. Tirzepatide, commonly branded as
body: Semaglutide, often marketed under the Ozempic and Wegovy banners, was first placed on Wada's monitoring list in 2024. Tirzepatide, commonly branded as Mounjaro, was added this year.For a substance to move from the monitoring list to the prohibited list, it needs to meet two of three criteria: that it can enhance sport performance, it poses a health risk to an athlete, or it violates the spirit of sport.Wada has started one study and is preparing another to examine the effects of the drugs in conditions designed to mimic high-level exercise."It's still going to take us a little bit of time to collect all this information, because they are highly controlled studies in very specific conditions," said Rabin."What we want to see is whether some of the pharmacological impact on human physiology that has been observed in obese patients would also occur in non-obese, highly trained people."Rabin said potential benefits could also be offset by side effects such as nausea, fatigue and the loss of muscle mass."If you're an athlete and you lose muscle mass, that may be very counterproductive for what you're trying to achieve," he said."So all these elements show you that it's not a very straightforward answer."Under the usual timetable, a change approved at next September's executive committee meeting would take effect in January 2028.Weight-loss drugs seem most likely to appeal to athletes in weight-category sports such as boxing and wrestling, as well as horse racing, where jockeys have to meet strict weight requirements."A lot of sports would benefit from weight control and weight management," said Rabin."Not only those in weight-category sports, but all sorts of sports."He highlighted long-distance runners and cyclists as other athletes with weight control "very high on their agenda"."There are sports as well where aesthetics play a role," he said. "It can be gymnastics, can be horse riding, can be many different sports where you don't have weight categories, but physical appearance is quite important."Very few athletes have spoken publicly about using weight-loss drugs. The most high-profile is Williams, who said she struggled to lose weight after having children.She is also a spokesperson for Ro, a company which sells GLP-1s and in which her husband is an investor.A recent Loughborough University study,, external which surveyed more than 100 sports medicine physicians around the world, found 12% were aware of athletes using GLP-1 drugs despite having no medical need for them.

schema.headline: Weight-loss drugs in sport: Ozempic, Mounjaro not on Wada banned list for athletes

title: Four killed and 60 injured in Russian strike on shopping centre, Ukraine says
description: Image source, State Emergency Service of UkraineByPatrick JacksonUkrainian officials say four people were killed and 60 wounded when a Russian drone a
body: Image source, State Emergency Service of UkraineByPatrick JacksonUkrainian officials say four people were killed and 60 wounded when a Russian drone attacked a shopping mall in Pavlohrad, a city in Dnipropetrovsk region.Shops and vehicles were hit in the daylight attack which took place "when the streets were full of people", Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said.Two other shopping malls - in the cities of Zaporizhzhia and Sumy - were targeted by Russian air strikes earlier this week, according to Ukrainian media.Russia reported a Ukrainian seaborne drone attack on the resort city of Sochi overnight on Wednesday, in which 28 people were wounded, as well as three more deaths blamed on Ukrainian attacks.A full-scale war has been raging between Russia and Ukraine since Russian President Vladimir Putin launched an invasion more than four and a half years ago.      A new peacemaking effort by envoys sent by US President Donald Trump at the weekend appears to have yielded few concrete results, after talks in Moscow with Putin and in Kyiv with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.   Images released by the State Emergency Service of Ukraine show firefighters directing water hoses at burning vehicles amid clouds of smoke on a street in Pavlohrad.Two of those injured are reported to be members of the service itself, and a child was also hurt.Zelensky offered his condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed in Thursday's attack. "The Russians used drones to kill people who were simply standing near shopping centres," Ukraine's president said in his statement.Pavlohrad, a logistics hub near the central city of Dnipro, has come under heavy attack previously, with two people killed in an attack on warehouses there last month.  Ukrainian officials say a Russian drone attack on a mall in Sumy on Wednesday killed two people and wounded 20. On Thursday, Russian aerial bombing reportedly injured eight people in Sumy, including three children. In Zaporizhzhia, capital of the region of the same name which was partially annexed by Russia soon after the invasion, a shopping mall was almost completely destroyed on Monday, its owners reported.However, it was closed at the time and there were no immediate reports of casualties.  One of the bloodiest attacks on a shopping centre came last month, when Ukrainian officials say Russian drones killed at least 16 people and injured 130 in the city of Kryvyi Rih.  Shopping malls in Russian-controlled parts of Ukraine have also come under attack, with a Ukrainian drone attack reported on Monday on a mall in the port city of Mariupol, Donetsk region, and another attack on the city of Donetsk last month.On Wednesday night, a number of Ukrainian seaborne drones attacked the shoreline at Sochi, Russian officials say. Two of the 28 people reported injured are children.On Thursday, Russian officials reported that a Ukrainian drone strike on the town of Novy Oskol in Belgord Region had killed one person and wounded six others.It was further announced that a Ukrainian attack on a car in Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia on Wednesday had killed a girl of 15, also injuring a child of six and two women; and a separate attack on a civilian lorry in the same region had killed a man.

schema.headline: Four killed and 60 injured in Russian strike on shopping centre, Ukraine says

title: New technology may bring more 9/11 victims' families closure
description: For 25 years, the only physical trace Juliette Scauso has had from the last day of her father's life was his mangled firefighter helmet.Scauso's fathe
body: For 25 years, the only physical trace Juliette Scauso has had from the last day of her father's life was his mangled firefighter helmet.Scauso's father, Dennis - part of a New York City Fire Department (FDNY) hazmat unit for 12 years -  initially was not scheduled to work on 11 September, 2001, but switched shifts for the overtime pay.The Long Island father of four was likely in the South Tower of the World Trade Center when it collapsed, the Scauso family was told. The helmet with his badge number was found months later."I've spent essentially my entire life knowing my father died, and learning to live with the fact that we never recovered him," said Scauso, who was four when he died.Dennis Scauso is one of more than 1,000 people killed on September 11 in New York who have yet to be identified, according to New York City's Office of Chief Medical Examiner. Nearly 3,000 people died in the World Trade Center attacks that day.Last month, the city announced the identity of a previously unknown victim of the terrorist attacks - the 1,654th person - using a new technology called forensic investigative genetic genealogy - or FIGG."There is real promise in using this approach," said Angela Soler, director of forensic anthropology in the city's medical examiner office. "There's hope for more families to receive answers, and hopefully we'll be able to test more remains in the future using this technology as well."Since 9/11, Soler's office has sought to identify the remains of the 2,753 victims who died in the World Trade Center. So far, 60 percent of those killed have been identified."It's been one of the most complex identification efforts that I think anybody has ever really experienced," Soler said.Efforts to identify victims have been complicated by a number of factors.Human remains were damaged in the plane crashes and fires caused by jet fuel, meaning the office had only portions of victims for DNA samples, Soler said.Scauso added that because of the timing of the attacks, many firefighters were changing shifts, but some stayed to help, grabbing whatever extra gear they could find. This meant some first responders recovered were wearing uniforms with others' names, complicating identification.The World Trade Center site also had many more victims than the other 9/11 terrorist attack sites.The remains of five of the 184 people killed when American Airlines Flight 77 crashed into the Pentagon were never identified because of similar conditions. According to the National Park Service, enough remains were recovered to use DNA, dental records and fingerprints to identify all 40 victims aboard United Airlines flight 93, which crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.Remains from the World Trade Center have been packaged and sealed to help preserve DNA for testing in the years to come. Soon after the attacks, individuals were identified using fingerprints or dental records, but as time went on, when neither was available, the office turned to DNA. Officials were able to use new technology to extract DNA and retest the same remains."That's why all these years down the road, we're still getting new identifications, because we're just continuing to retest and retry with every new technology that becomes available," Soler said.DNA technology has helped the office identify 1,495 victims since 9/11 - some solely with DNA and others with multiple methods - according to the medical examiner's office.Last year, the city announced that with the help of DNA, 24 years later, it had identified three new victims - Ryan Fitzgerald, a 26-year-old currency trader, Babara Keating, a 72-year-old who was aboard American Airlines Flight 11 from Boston to Los Angeles, and a woman whose family kept her identity private.Soler said the new FIGG technology uses whole genome sequencing - which provides a way to read someone's entire genetic code. It means investigators can make more potential matches to family members who are more distant relatives of the victim. Once those matches are made, the New York Police Department helps find relatives who are closer to the victims.The medical examiner's office in New York still gets weekly calls from loved ones asking about someone whose remains were never recovered.Many have never been able to bury a loved one, but some families choose to leave the remains - once found - at a repository at the 9/11 memorial site in New York. The repository was built into the bedrock of the World Trade Center site and can only be accessed by medical examiner staff. A nearby private space, known as the reflection room, is available for families to mourn."That's where their loved one was in their last moments, and that's where they want them to stay", Soler said.Some don't want to be notified, perhaps because the confirmation is too painful, said Soler, who helps inform families.Scauso is one of those people. She knows people who, in recent years, got a call that a relative finally has been identified. The thought of being next on the list is scary for her family, who has worked hard to keep the memory of her father - a jack of all trades and a lover of jazz - alive."At this point, an identification wouldn't change the reality of his death. It wouldn't give me back my father, and I don't necessarily want to reopen something that has become part of the way I've learned to live and grieve," she said. "Especially 25 years later, it's going to open up the wounds again."But, Scauso said, the technology is important.Soler has seen the news provide a mix of both relief and sadness. "It's confirmation of something that they always knew to be true - they knew their loved one died on 9/11, but I think for many families, there's still that question in the back of their mind until the remains are formally identified," Soler said."Maybe they're reliving it a little bit more now, having this new identification. But at the same time, it closes one chapter of their journey after 9/11," she added.To Soler - and some of her current colleagues who also were on the ground during 9/11 - the work is deeply personal. Workers from their office arrived at Ground Zero after the planes hit the towers, and were there when the buildings collapsed.They are aware it is unlikely they will identify every victim of the New York attacks. In some instances, there may be no remains of a victim at all. Still, they have no plans to stop."As long as there's families looking for answers, we'll continue searching for them," she said.

schema.headline: New technology may bring more 9/11 victims' families closure

title: Use all powers necessary on anti-migrant protests, home secretary tells police
description: "These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious mal
body: "These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents," the Home Secretary said."This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons."The BBC understands that police chiefs are now actively considering using recently-granted powers to completely ban face coverings in specific areas, in light of that demonstration.Saturday's protest was followed 24 hours later with another in which men blocked the only road out of Langstone Harbour, near Portsmouth, after the RNLI had brought ashore 120 migrants.It's unclear at this stage whether further such protests will go ahead - but in some areas of England local groups that have associated themselves with the Patriot Platform umbrella group have called for more demonstrations.The meeting discussed the emergence of Patriot Platform with ministers believing the group aims to intimidate communities.Mahmood is said to have told police chiefs to make better use of intelligence to make sure they had better plans in place ahead of this weekend.That call came after Kent Police had earlier admitted it had been made aware of a potential demonstration in Dover but had not "fully assessed" the warning before the town's nationally critical port road was brought to a standstill.During the meeting, Mahmood is said to have made clear the government expected police to make full use of powers and to deal robustly with any criminal offences.Speaking after the meeting, Deputy Chief Constable Andy Mariner, the National Police Chiefs Council lead for public order, said forces were "continually assessing and preparing for protests and any potential impact on public safety".This includes working closely with "local forces, specialist teams, communities and partners" to ensure support is available when needed.He added: "Our priority is to keep people safe, maintain public order and support the right to peaceful and lawful protest. While people are entitled to express their views, anyone committing criminal offences can and should expect police action."Major changes to protest law in the last three years mean officers can now intervene more quickly to end demonstrations that block critical national infrastructure, such as roads to ports.They can also designate an entire area a face mask-free zone for the duration of a protest.It's that second power that police chiefs are now considering using.Police chiefs also say they have initiated an "enhanced and co-ordinated" approach to gathering as much intelligence as possible in the days ahead.

schema.headline: Use all powers necessary on anti-migrant protests, home secretary tells police

title: Alice Kinsella: British gymnast continues historic comeback at international level
description: Olympic gymnast Alice Kinsella says it is "hard to put into words" how she feels about returning to international competition as her groundbreaking co
body: Olympic gymnast Alice Kinsella says it is "hard to put into words" how she feels about returning to international competition as her groundbreaking comeback to the sport continues this weekend.The two-time European champion became the first British artistic gymnast to resume elite competition after giving birth, when she finished fourth in the beam at the British Championships in March.Now the 25-year-old is preparing for her first competition back in Great Britain colours at a senior team international against France, Switzerland, Germany and Italy at Fenton Manor in Stoke on 12-13 September."It's kind of crazy - it's such a surreal feeling but I am very excited," Kinsella told BBC Radio Stoke."It's only been a year, postpartum. Training-wise, it's been tough, but it's been good.  I'm excited to finally get out there. I'm ready, I'm doing everything I can to get back where I was."It's been a rollercoaster but a good one."Kinsella's pioneering journey back to the sport is so rare it became the subject of a university research paper into elite gymnasts resuming their careers after giving birth.Her son Parker, who was born in September 2025, is already a source of inspiration and he will be watching his mum compete at the weekend as Kinsella competes in all four pieces of apparatus - balance beam, bars, vault and floor - for the first time."It's really special because I've wanted to try to get back into a team and this is a really good start because it's a little four-way," said Kinsella, who trains with Park Wrekin Gymnastics Club in Shropshire."It's not too big of a competition, which is really good. I'm definitely nervous, but it's hard to put into words - it's been so long."I did the British [Championships] in March but only did beam and that's all I was training really, but now I'm trying to do all four so it's more on the body."It's not like you've done one piece and you can stop thinking about everything, you've got to move on to the next and think about that. So it's been tough."After revealing she only took "three or four weeks off" after giving birth, Kinsella returned to training at the start of the year with the longer-term intention of being at the World Championships in China in 2027 and the Olympics in Los Angeles in 2028.But, after finding herself ahead of schedule so far this year, she wanted to take the chance to step it up."My main goal was to try to get back next year but I'm actually a lot further forward than I thought I would be," added Kinsella, who won bronze in the team event at the Tokyo Olympics in 2020."So that's why I'm doing this competition because I just want to get out there, compete, because I don't like doing nothing."What makes Kinsella's return so unique are the obvious challenges - and changes to the body - pregnancy and childbirth brings.There are many examples of women returning to the top of their sports after becoming mothers but gymnastics, where vital pelvic floor and core strength are both weakened during pregnancy, is different.Kinsella said her gymnastics background has played a big part in her being able to return to physical exercise so quickly but said she "didn't feel too bad" when she got back in the gym."I always had that goal to get back into the gym and I think when I've got a goal set I will do everything I can to achieve it," she said."Getting back into a leotard with how my body's changed just feels very weird, but I guess that shows what my body has gone through and I try to think about it in a positive way."Her body is not the only thing that has changed with Kinsella adding that parenthood has helped her become better at taking the pressure off herself as an athlete."Having a baby changes your life - I'm very patient, whereas before Parker I was not patient at all," she said."When I made one tiny mistake I would get so annoyed, but now if I just make like a little mistake I'm totally fine about it."You have to be patient with kids, they're crazy. So I've definitely changed in that aspect but style-wise and gymnastics-wise like I don't think that's changed."Things are harder to get back and to do but I think the more I train it'll probably feel a lot easier."Kinsella said when she started her comeback "no one really had any idea what I was going to able to do" and wants to keep levels of expectation for her international return as realistic as possible.For her, this weekend in Stoke is there primarily "just to enjoy it" and to "get the experience of all four pieces [of apparatus] again"."My body's changed, I can't do the same amount of training I used to do but I'm definitely getting back to that," Kinsella said."We're definitely on the right track to be where I was before I had Parker. My goal was to start competing next year properly on all four. "It's going to be really fun. Whatever happens, happens, good, bad. I'm just proud I'm able to be back out there a year postpartum."

schema.headline: Alice Kinsella: British gymnast continues historic comeback at international level

title: Wiltshire teacher sexually abused pupils at multiple schools
description: "James manipulated her victims with calculated precision, exploiting her position of authority to isolate them and normalise the abuse," she added."Th
body: "James manipulated her victims with calculated precision, exploiting her position of authority to isolate them and normalise the abuse," she added."This was not a lapse in judgement; it was a sustained pattern of predatory behaviour against children in her care."A spokesperson from the NSPCC said James had "exploited" a "position of trust" where she was supposed to "support, protect and educate those in her professional care". "When someone in authority abuses a trusted relationship, young people can find it particularly difficult to recognise what is happening or to speak out about it, and it can have a profound and lasting impact on their wellbeing," they added. A spokesperson from Hardenhuish School said they "commend" the courage of the young people who came forward to give evidence in the case."The safety and wellbeing of our pupils is, and always will be, our highest priority," they said.They added that safeguarding arrangements are regularly reviewed and recruitment processes are in line with government guidance."We continue to work closely with Wiltshire Council and other safeguarding partners to ensure that the highest standards of safeguarding are maintained across the school."

schema.headline: Wiltshire teacher sexually abused pupils at multiple schools

title: Air traffic chaos and compensation: 'Shutdown cost us more than £1,000'
description: Catie, 30, and Phil, 34, were sat on a British Airways flight to Ljubljana on Tuesday that never took off. If a flight is cancelled, airlines must get
body: Catie, 30, and Phil, 34, were sat on a British Airways flight to Ljubljana on Tuesday that never took off. If a flight is cancelled, airlines must get customers to their destination as quickly as possible at no extra cost, even if it is with a rival carrier.Alternatively, passengers can take a refund, which should also be offered for flight delays of more than five hours.In Catie and Phil's case, the alternative flight offered would not have arrived until Saturday morning - four days into their week-long holiday. So they took the refund. That was not easy. The chatbot only seemed to allow them to rebook, and it took more than an hour waiting to speak to BA on the phone before the refund was confirmed. It will take a week to be paid.When airlines are at fault, extra compensation is paid under UK and EU rules. But not this time, because the air traffic control issues were beyond airlines' control. Even so, airlines themselves are furious that they have been saddled with a bill of millions of pounds.BA also refunded the couple's car hire, which had been organised through the airline. The problem for the couple was that they had booked accommodation and excursions separately, and that is money they have lost.

schema.headline: Air traffic chaos and compensation: 'Shutdown cost us more than £1,000'

title: Primark finally set to launch online deliveries
description: Primark has said it plans to launch a home delivery service in Britain, four years after it made its first foray into e-commerce.The retailer did not
body: Primark has said it plans to launch a home delivery service in Britain, four years after it made its first foray into e-commerce.The retailer did not say when it expects to launch the service, but it has bought a warehouse in Sheffield to enable it to ship products to homes.The company said there was "opportunity for profitable growth" through home deliveries, which could help boost trade after Primark reported subdued sales following the recent hot weather.Analysts said the decision to offer home delivery after years of resistance - including through the pandemic - indicated that Primark was facing major challenges from ultra-fast-fashion brands such as Shein.Primark did not sell goods online until 2022, when it launched a click-and-collect service which meant shoppers still had to travel to pick up their purchases. Associated British Foods (ABF), which owns Primark, said the fashion chain would "continue to grow click and collect and... will in the future offer home delivery in Great Britain".ABF predicts Primark's UK sales will grow by about 1% in the fourth quarter of the year. But like-for-like sales - a key metric in the retail industry, which strips out the impact of store openings and closures - are expected to be "broadly flat" in the UK, and fall 3% across its global operations.It said sales of autumn/winter clothing started later than normal due to the hot weather in the summer, but "trading was stronger when the weather cooled towards the end of the quarter".The fast-fashion chain is struggling to compete with brands such as Shein and Boohoo, as well as alternative platforms such as TikTok Shop and Vinted, and in July said it was lowering prices on hundreds of clothing items. Retail analyst Julie Palmer said that "Primark has been playing catch up for years" and launching home deliveries "is as much about defence as growth".She told BBC News that "the real test" for the brand is whether it can make home deliveries profitable at the low prices customers have come to expect from fast fashion chains."Shein and Vinted have already reset customer expectations on convenience," she said, adding that a "slick and effective returns policy" will also be key.ABF is planning to spin off Primark from its food business next year. Retail analyst Natalie Berg said Primark was "more than fashionably late to the e-commerce party".She said the brand will need to absorb additional costs of returns, which tend to be higher than in-store purchases as customers cannot try clothes on before buying them."Not even the pandemic could convince them to launch online, so the fact that Primark is making such a U-turn tells us just how much the retail landscape has evolved," she said.Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said that thanks to greater competition among delivery firms such as InPost and Relay, "it's become a lot cheaper in the past few years to send items by post, compared to the old days when Royal Mail dominated the market", he added.Retailers across the UK are grappling with higher costs for labour and energy.On Thursday, John Lewis - which operates the department stores and Waitrose supermarkets - reported that its half-year losses had widened to £124m from £88m a year earlier.Chairman Jason Tarry said the results reflected the partnership's "continued investment in our transformation, a more challenging trading environment and the increased costs of doing business".Sales in the department store arm of the business fell 2%, as it said consumers were holding back on discretionary spending. Waitrose sales were up 4%, but profits slipped slightly which the company said was due to a decision to lower prices and also reflected "the extra cost of running our operations through the heatwaves".

schema.headline: Primark finally set to launch online deliveries

title: Solheim Cup 2026: Charley Hull to face Nelly Korda in opening foursomes match
description: Europe's Charley Hull and Lottie Woad will face the formidable pairing of Nelly Korda and Allisen Corpuz in Friday's opening match of the Solheim Cup
body: Europe's Charley Hull and Lottie Woad will face the formidable pairing of Nelly Korda and Allisen Corpuz in Friday's opening match of the Solheim Cup in the Netherlands.While English pair Woad and Hull are seventh and eighth in the rankings, the American duo have won all four of their foursomes matches across the past two editions of the contest.  That included a victory over Hull and Esther Henseleit in the first match of the 2024 edition. "Charley and Lottie, they've got to play [together] quite a bit on tour this year, so I think they were both very excited to be paired with each other," said Europe's captain Anna Nordqvist."If you are going to be anywhere [on Friday morning] you want to be on the first tee because it doesn't get better than that."US captain Angela Stanford, added: "If I didn't put those two out [Korda and Corpuz], I would be questioned. I feel like the whole world knew that they were coming."We can talk about Nelly and we can talk about her being the number one player in the world, but don't sleep on Allisen. I've called her the backbone of our team. "She's pretty tough. There are a lot of good things going on in that pairing that, you know, they just complement each other really well."Play gets under way at Bernardus Golf at 06:40 BST with four foursomes (alternate shot) matches.

schema.headline: Solheim Cup 2026: Charley Hull to face Nelly Korda in opening foursomes match

title: Bromley stabbing: One man in critical condition as seven arrested
description: Four hurt and seven arrested in Bromley stabbingImage source, PA MediaImage caption, KFC confirmed that a "serious incident" took place at the restaur
body: Four hurt and seven arrested in Bromley stabbingImage source, PA MediaImage caption, KFC confirmed that a "serious incident" took place at the restaurant ByAmy ClarkeUpdated 5 minutes agoSeven people have been arrested after four men were stabbed in south-east London, the Metropolitan Police has said.One of the men remains in a critical condition in hospital, while the other three are being treated for injuries that are not believed to be life-threatening.Paramedics and the London Air Ambulance were called at about 14:20 BST to Bromley High Street, where one eyewitness reported seeing a man wielding a machete.A KFC spokesperson confirmed a "serious incident" had taken place at its Bromley High Street restaurant and an altercation had begun there. The company said it was assisting police and "supporting our team members and customers at this difficult time".Image caption, Paramedics were sent to Bromley High Street on Thursday afternoonAn eyewitness, who did not want to be named, said: "I saw a fight breaking out at the door of KFC; people involved were partly inside and outside."A male in a grey tracksuit pulled out a machete and ran further into KFC holding it up in the air, at which point most people around KFC started running away, including my friend and I."I didn't turn around until we got to the shopping centre where I saw him running away with someone down a road."Image source, @Vinnie_VdkImage caption, Police said there was no wider threat to the publicGeorgiana, the manager of Merkur Slots gambling shop, said she saw "a fight spill out" on to the High Street.She said she became "very worried", and locked three customers inside the premises to wait for the situation to calm down.She said the customers remained inside and that the shop was still closed.Figure caption, Watch: BBC reports from scene of south-east London stabbingVinnie Guadagnino, who lives on Bromley High Street, said he saw a large emergency response with multiple police cars and about 10 officers on foot."Police cars kept coming, then within the next half hour there were multiple fire engines and people gathering."Then there was a drone overhead and helicopters and an air ambulance - so a massive emergency service response."Image caption, A cordon remains in place at the sceneBromley High Street is currently closed both ways from Ringers Road to Ethelbert Road.Police remain at the scene and say there is not believed to be any wider threat to the public.Image source, PAImage caption, Forensic investigators at the scene on Bromley High StreetPeter Fortune, Conservative MP for Bromley and Biggin Hill, said on X that residents "would have safety concerns" and he would remain in contact with the police as they investigate.Liberal Democrat councillor Graeme Casey said: "We're very grateful because, of course, one of the big problems we have in London is our police are quite thinly stretched, so to have had such a robust response in such a short space of time is really to the credit of all the blue-light services involved."Image caption, Witnesses Matias Alil and Fergal Hickey saw the commotion Matias Alil described the reaction on the street. He said: "It was terrible. We saw a massive commotion and something going on in KFC. It was really scary, to be honest."Fergal Hickey added: "You can see the police out there have the situation under control, so you don't really need to be too anxious about it but it's still pretty crazy to see it when it happens."Get in touchWere you in the area? Did you witness the incident? If it is safe to do so, please get in touch.

schema.headline: Bromley stabbing: One man in critical condition as seven arrested

title: 'My cancer spread while I waited 128 days for an op':  The cost of England's care gap
description: Alan was diagnosed with lung cancer after a nodule was found in June last year.The 70-year-old was meant to be operated on within weeks but ended up w
body: Alan was diagnosed with lung cancer after a nodule was found in June last year.The 70-year-old was meant to be operated on within weeks but ended up waiting nearly five months, by which time the cancer had spread, making his surgery more complex."I was so frustrated and angry and couldn't understand why they would leave me like that," says Alan.On two occasions, scans were cancelled because machines had broken and for weeks he heard little or nothing from the hospital about when he would eventually have the urgent surgery.Alan is one of thousands each month in England who are not being treated within the target timeframe.Earlier this year, the government's National Cancer Plan, along with the NHS Planning Guidance, set out that 80% of patients in England would start treatment within 62 days from urgent GP referral by March 2027. This was to reach 85% by March 2029.But in the months since the government announced this ambition, performance has got worse, according to NHS England data, not better.Now, 71.2% of patients start cancer treatment within the 62 day timeframe. Previously it was 71.9%.Radiotherapy UK analysis, shared exclusively with the BBC, suggests more than 2,800 extra patients would need to start treatment every month - a near 15% increase on current numbers - to achieve the March 2027 target.That is likely to grow as referrals keep rising across nearly every cancer type.Price says thousands of patients "are going to die unnecessarily, just because the government can't get their act together to treat people on time".  For every month a cancer patient waits before starting treatment, their chance of survival falls by around 10%, on average.By the time Alan had his operation, the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes and the nodule "had grown at an alarming rate", according to the lung specialist.He has since been told the cancer has cleared awaiting his one-year review, but the operation has left him in debilitating pain. "I used to play golf and get out and about. Now I can't do any of the things I love," says Alan.Roughly 54,000 more patients will need to start treatment within 62 days before 2029 for the government to hit its goal.One NHS trust that is gaining traction on its waiting list numbers is Salisbury, but it is still not hitting targets.  Staff say there is no single fix, just a relentless focus on getting the basics right; making sure patients know about their appointments and turn up, keeping IT systems working, recruiting the right people, making sure surgical lists are full and expanding capacity.Much of the visible progress has come through skin and prostate cancer, two of the most common cancers in the country.But staff in Salisbury also say missed appointments, whether down to late letters, illness, transport problems or anxiety, are a constant drain on a system already stretched thin.Emilia Scutt, cancer manager in Salisbury, says that efforts to reduce missed appointments have really helped their numbers."We know cancer can be terrifying so we are a bit like a dog with the bone, backing up patients and supporting them wherever we can."Trusts with the sharpest declines in performance - including Buckinghamshire Healthcare, Bolton NHS Foundation Trust, Royal Devon University Healthcare Trust, East Cheshire, and Torbay and South Devon - told the BBC they face pressures across the board. Rising demand, workforce shortages and diagnostic bottlenecks have all played a part.Some pointed to industrial action and staff sickness, others to reliance on outside diagnostic providers or major changes to how their systems work. All say they are investing in extra capacity, working through backlogs and redesigning pathways, and are already seeing early signs of improvement."If government is serious about delivering on the ambitions of the National Cancer Plan for England, it must match ambition with urgency," said Steve Haines of Macmillan Cancer Support.He said that "visible progress" was needed on a promise to set up a National Cancer Board to oversee progress on improving waiting times and treatment.A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson says "cancer waiting times are moving in the right direction will all three cancer standards better than a year ago".They concede that "there is more to do," and that the plan "will help people get diagnosed earlier and begin treatment sooner."Additional reporting Daniel Wainwright and Jess Carr

schema.headline: 'My cancer spread while I waited 128 days for an op':  The cost of England's care gap

title: Oil, gas and borrowing costs surge as fears over Middle East escalate
description: The price of oil has jumped to $105 a barrel amid signs the conflict in the Middle East will not be resolved quickly, fuelling fears that inflation co
body: The price of oil has jumped to $105 a barrel amid signs the conflict in the Middle East will not be resolved quickly, fuelling fears that inflation could accelerate. With the conflict between the US and Iran in the Gulf intensifying in recent days, the cost of both crude oil and gas has been rising sharply. Brent crude went back above $100 a barrel on Wednesday and has continued to climb.The war has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, preventing supplies of oil and gas from the Gulf from reaching global markets.US and UK long-term borrowing costs also surged to their highest level in decades.Speaking at a Republican Party convention in Texas on Wednesday, President Trump said he did not think the fighting would end until after the US mid-term elections in November. Analysts said the combination of rising energy costs and higher borrowing costs was adding pressure on financial markets. Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at trading platform IG, said investors were becoming increasingly concerned about the economic impact of higher oil prices. "It feels like investors worldwide are now waking up to the crisis in oil markets," Beauchamp said. He warned that the surge in energy prices could weigh heavily on the global economy if it continues. Concerns have also grown after Iran-aligned Houthi forces were reported to have seized Yemen's port of Mokha, a key Red Sea port.The move could elevate fears of further shipping disruptions.The price of natural gas has also been soaring on wholesale markets. In the UK, it rose above 200p a therm for the first time since the end of 2022.Storage levels in Europe are much lower than normal for the time of year, and the need to fill reserves ahead of the winter has helped to push up prices.

title: Pilot warned Amazon cargo plane going too fast before deadly crash, data shows
description: The flight data released by NTSB included the plane's speed, altitude, and other details like flap deployment as it approached the runway. The update
body: The flight data released by NTSB included the plane's speed, altitude, and other details like flap deployment as it approached the runway. The update also included the summary of conversation between the two pilots.The summary noted the pilot's cautions about speed occurred "throughout the remainder of the recording" as did the inconsistent verbal response. The update said there was an electronic "sink rate sink rate" callout during the final minutes - an automated safety warning about the speed of descent.There was also an ​electronic "too low terrain" callout, another automated verbal warning that the plane was flying too close to the ground without being properly prepared for landing.Aviation attorney Pablo Rojas told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that it was difficult to know without the actual recording what the NTSB was referring to when it noted the inconsistent verbal response."But, it really confirms that this was, in a way, a doomed approach," he said. Rojas noted that flap deployment data included in NTSB's update also could be an area of concern. The flaps, located on the back of the wings,  are "part of what helps the plane kind of slow down and gently approach a landing", he said. "The flap deployment here happened much later in the accident sequence," Rojas said. "That's maybe because the pilots were responding to the fact that they were going too fast."After it overshot the runway, the plane - Amazon Prime Air Flight 7598 - struck equipment on the ground, hit a white Ford van, then continued onward through a perimeter fence. It then collided with a Toyota Corolla, before coming to rest about 1,300ft (394m) beyond the runway. The five who died were part of a plane-cleaning crew in the van. Miami authorities on Tuesday identified them as Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Julio C Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47.

title: Yemen's Houthis reportedly seize strategic Red Sea port of Mokha
description: Yemen's Houthis have seized the strategic Red Sea port city of Mokha from Saudi-backed pro-government forces, military sources and witnesses say.Mokha
body: Yemen's Houthis have seized the strategic Red Sea port city of Mokha from Saudi-backed pro-government forces, military sources and witnesses say.Mokha's capture leaves the Iran-backed group only 75km (46 miles) away from the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gateway to a trade route that links Asia and Europe.The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping but reiterated their threat to target vessels from Saudi Arabia, which has relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.The escalation of the conflict between the Houthis, Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia has contributed to a surge in oil prices.Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed and thousands displaced since the Houthis launched an offensive in the south-west a week ago.A Saudi-led coalition has also carried out air strikes on Houthi-controlled areas in western Yemen in support of the pro-government forces, and the Houthis have launched missiles and drones at cities and oil facilities in southern Saudi Arabia.Mokha residents said Houthi fighters moved into the city after fierce clashes with pro-government forces on Wednesday night, prompting many families to flee their homes."The takeover came without warning. Panic spread throughout the area, forcing people to flee amid distressing scenes of injured people lying in the streets with no-one there to help them," one man told BBC Arabic's Middle East Lifeline programme.Another man said that Houthi fighters were patrolling the streets of Mokha on Thursday, while government offices and shops were closed."At the moment, we don't know what Ansar Allah will do," he added, using the group's formal name. "Everyone is afraid for their safety."Many displaced families are heading east towards the city of Aden, where Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council and government are based."We fled with our children and kept running. We have no bedding, no home, nothing with us. Everything was destroyed within an hour. They didn't even give us a chance or warn us beforehand," one woman told BBC Arabic."We are women with no means of defending ourselves, and we have innocent children with us."There was no immediate confirmation of Mokha's capture from the Houthis.But the group's Supreme Political Council said in a statement on Thursday that clashes had "ceased in the western coast districts after the expulsion of Saudi enemy mobilisations", according to Houthi-run Al Masirah TV.Tarek Salah, leader of the pro-government National Resistance Forces, also said he had moved his command centre on the west coast to a "safe location".He added that his forces had paid "a heavy price in recent days in the face of a Houthi offensive that was planned and supported by Iran".A Yemeni military source told AFP news agency that Houthi fighters had also seized Zuqar Island in the Red Sea, about 80km north-west of Mokha, after launching a barrage of rockets and a ground assault using boats.Meanwhile, the head of the Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, urged Arab states and other countries to help protect Yemen's coasts and restore state control.The Houthis' Supreme Political Council asserted its "right to defend [Yemen's] sovereignty and territorial waters while simultaneously reassuring the international community that navigation in the Red Sea remains safe".However, the Houthi-run humanitarian operations co-ordination centre also stressed that the embargo on Saudi ships remained in place.Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said Saudi warplanes carried out 64 strikes across the western provinces of Taiz, Hudaydah, Marib and Jawf over the previous 24 hours.There was no immediate comment from the Saudi military.However, the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states fighting in Yemen said on Wednesday evening that it would respond to a series of Houthi missile and drone attacks on the south-western Saudi cities of Khamis Mushait, Abha and Jazan.On Tuesday, the Houthis launched dozens of drones and missiles at southern Saudi Arabia, injuring 73 civilians and causing fires at several oil facilities that led to a temporary halt in operations, according to Saudi authorities.The Houthis said they were retaliating for dozens of Saudi air strikes on territory they control in recent days, including one on a prison in the town of Hazm in Jawf province on Monday that they said killed at least 23 civilians.The Saudi-led coalition has backed Yemen's government against the Houthis in the country's devastating civil war for more than a decade.A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

schema.headline: Yemen's Houthis reportedly seize strategic Red Sea port of Mokha
